utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is Case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances for the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Matthias Neuner, Aditya Menon, and our case manager Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Vasvija Vidovic with Nicholas Robson for the Defence, with Lejla Gluhic and Lana Deljkic as assistants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Delalic, may I just remind you that you're still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much. Any questions arising from questions from the Bench for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have, Your Honours; with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Madam Vidovic, and you may be seated. Further Cross-examination by Madam Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Delalic. I'm going to ask you a few more questions. Before the questions asked by Their Honours in your yesterday's testimony, you never mentioned that the Mujahedin were fighting side by side with you on the 8th of June, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you mention it or didn't you mention it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. His Honour, Judge Moloto, page 97, lines 23 to 95, and page 98, lines 1 to 4 of unofficial transcripts, suggested to you the following: "If they did not operate together with you, it was your duty, as the Bosnian Army, to protect those that you were guarding; is that so?" Your answer was: "We protected them, as far as I know, but if we failed in so doing --" But you failed to finish your answer. You were interrupted by His Honour Judge Moloto asking you the following: "Given that you omitted to provide protection for them, you are legally liable; is that correct?" And then a little bit further on on the same page, lines 11 to 13 on the same page, the question was: "Given the BH Army also has legal liability to secure safety for these people, and if there were not --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are asked to speak slowly because the interpreter is not able to cope up with you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise both to you and the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you now is the following: The BH Army, at the beginning of the war, adopted its own rules relating to command responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It did not apply the rules of the former Yugoslav People's Army but rather their own rules of engagement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to the BH Army rules that you, yourself, working in the security applied, the army commanders were able only to prosecute their subordinate if they commit any crimes; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt my learned friend, but if she could please explain what the relevance or what the relationship between her current line of questioning and the Judge's questioning is, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond to this. Your Honours asked the witness about the legal responsibility for ensuring the safety of those men, and there couldn't be any more direct link than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But you're referring here to the rules of the JNA and so on. What is the direct relationship?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I mentioned the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted its own rules instead of applying the JNA rules, because the issue here is the responsibility of the army for the crimes committed, and the witness was working in security and in the process applied these rules, and this directly stems from the question asked by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So my last question was about the army rules that you, yourselves, being involved in security, applied. The army commanders were entitled only to prosecute their subordinates if they committed any crimes; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, it was your duty to investigate whether any subordinates was a member of your unit and committed a crime and thereby undertake certain measures against such a person if he did that; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this particular circumstances, that is, the events of the 8th of June, 1994, you established that your subordinates had not committed a crime, but rather that it was committed by the Mujahedin; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not consider them your subordinates; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And they were not subordinate to you for that matter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean you were not -- they were not subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You reported about this to your superior command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that the civilian police was also notified about this incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, you also said that the civilian police had filed a criminal report against an unidentified perpetrator; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, just one minor issue. You had learned about the abduction of the victims being done in the most brutal way by members of your unit's military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At least one of these policemen had -- Your Honour, my colleague has drawn my attention to page 5, lines 23 to 25, again that the abduction was carried out by members of your units. Can we please clarify this, Witness? The Mujahedin abducted, in the most brutal way, the prisoners from the people who were escorting this group of prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: One of them had a rifle barrel put in his mouth. That was one of your military policemen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This policeman, as a result of shock, has fallen ill, seriously ill, and he never recovered; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I can just ask my learned colleague again the last two or three questions, how did they arise out of the questions of the Judges? We are talking here about facts of the abduction, that rifles are put into the mouth of others. I don't see a link to the Judge's questions here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer, Your Honours? There was mention of the measures taken against the abductors, and the witness responded to your questions about the possibility of providing security to the victims. We are talking here now about the possibility for the army to do something about this, and this also directly stems from the question the Bench has asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I think in his examination-in-chief and also not in your cross-examination, the witness has not touched the witness in what details threats during the abduction had been carried out or not. This is an issue which could have been covered on cross-examination, if necessary, and I believe we are now taking the Judge's questions a little bit too far in trying to establish these facts at this late point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honours. The witness, in response to your yesterday's question, tried to explain that they did everything that it was possible to be done, that everything possible was done by this Army of the BH -- of this unit of the BH Army, and this is the basis for my question. So they did everything possible in order to provide the protection for the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, if you have questions after your learned colleague has finished, you may put questions to the witness, too. You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you indeed have questions, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: No further questions at this point in time. Thank you to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Delalic. This brings us to the end of this testimony. On behalf of the Trial Chamber and the Chamber, I would just like to take the opportunity to thank you for testifying and taking time off your busy schedule. You are now excused. You may stand down, and may you travel safely back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. As a result of questions put by the Judges in respect of this last witness, I'd be very grateful for the opportunity just to raise a few points in clarification for the record, if I may. At the outset, if I could say that yet again the Defence readily accepts that the Trial Chamber is entitled to seek clarification from the witnesses, it appears, is also entitled to put questions with the aim of finding out the truth of the matters that it hears. However, it is the Defence's submission that a number of questions were put to the witness that did not necessarily reflect the applicable law, nor the evidence previously given by the witness during his examination-in-chief and cross-examination on the transcript. And in such a situation we feel obliged to raise these concerns to avoid the possibility of the Defence being criticised at a later stage for not making its position known to the Trial Chamber. So it's with that in mind that I raise these points. The first point relates to the suggestion put several times by Your Honour Judge Moloto, that following the kidnapping by the Mujahedin of the Bosnian Croat detainees from the ABiH, that the army owed a legal duty to pursue the Mujahedin. The Defence would accept that where a party to a conflict detains persons, whether they be civilians or prisoners of war, then a duty of care would indeed arise towards those detainees. That is clear. However, in a situation where a third party intervenes and removes those detainees from the control of that party, we do not accept necessarily that a duty to pursue exists either in international law or in Bosnian domestic law. From the questions put by Your Honour, it was a little unclear to us, but it may be the case that the Trial Chamber has already made a determination, number one, that a legal duty to pursue did indeed exist at that time and, number two, that there was, in fact, a failure by members of the ABiH to comply with that legal duty and pursue the Mujahedin. If the Trial Chamber has indeed made such a determination, it's not clear to us what the consequences of such a breach of duty by the ABiH could be. We would just like to note for the record that in the amended indictment upon which General Delic is charged, he is not charged with criminal responsibility in respect of a failure by his subordinates to pursue those Mujahedin. Your Honours, that's the first point. The second point I can deal with briefly. Again, this arises out of a further question put by Your Honour Judge Moloto. Your Honour put to the witness that those people who actually kidnapped the civilians or the prisoners of war, they had actually been fighting side by side with the enemy. We've obviously heard evidence about the events on the 8th of June, but the Defence would just like to record that this witness, at no time during his earlier testimony, mentioned that the Mujahedin or the persons wearing masks that accompanied them had actually been fighting in the Bila Valley that day, and for the record it's our understanding from the testimony of other Prosecution witnesses, no such evidence has been given as well. So, Your Honour, those are my submissions, as I say, as a matter of clarification for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you asking for a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Trial Chamber would like to respond, we would certainly appreciate that, but we're not necessarily expecting you to respond at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to respond. I would like just to say that on the first point, the Trial Chamber has made no determination of any issue, either in law or in fact, at this stage. On the second point, I just want to say to you I don't think it was ever put to the witness that he testified to the fact that the Mujahedin fought side by side, so the question was not dependent on the testimony of the witness, himself. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I have an idea that I would like to share with the parties, because during the witnesses we have heard, mention has frequently been made to -- a reference has frequently been made to the organisation of the 3rd Corps, and I wonder if the Bench could ask either the Prosecution or both parties, really, to get together and agree on a chart, an organisational chart, which would show how the 3rd Corps was really organised. And of course also the level of command from the 3rd Corps up to the Supreme Commander, the accused. In particular, I am not sure about just what the relation is between the 306th Brigade and the 7th Muslim Brigade, nor am I completely sure about the division of responsibility between the 306th Brigade and the 314th Brigade, so I would be happy to see, what do you call it, the organograms of how this was organised and who was in charge of each of these brigades and battalions, if that is possible. That would be of great assistance to the Bench. I assume that it would be the responsibility of the Prosecution to produce such a map. However, I would be unhappy if the Defence would feel that this was being impressed upon them, upon you. So we can either ask the Prosecution to bring us a draft and then you can comment on it, or if you have time, to cooperate on the production of this piece of evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just state that there may be a number of matters in dispute concerning the organisation between the parties, but we'll obviously endeavour to see what common ground there is and see if we can produce something useful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Exactly. That was exactly the reason why I suggested some sort of cooperation, and we would be perfectly happy if the differences between the parties could be somehow highlighted when you make this organogram. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I appreciate the issue that Judge Harhoff has raised, and I can assure the Chamber that I will endeavour to produce such an organogram in cooperation with the Defence. I will also undertake a review of the material that was admitted in the Hadzihasanovic case, as of course General Hadzihasanovic was the 3rd Corps Commander for the majority of 1993, and there may very well be some documents or organograms that were admitted in that case that we can also present to the Defence and perhaps to the Trial Chamber. We will endeavour to present that material as soon as we're able to identify it and speak with the Defence about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Have you got the next witness, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution calls Murat Softic, and my colleague, Mr. Menon, will be leading the examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You may be seated. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, could you please indicate your full name, your date of birth, and your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: My name is Murat Softic. I was born on the 12th of October, 1948.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Sjeverin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Softic, were you ever a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when did you join the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: After I finished my academy in 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you leave the JNA at a certain point?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I left it in late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what did you do when you left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I joined the resistance in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Did you at some point join the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, immediately after its induction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And for how long were you a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly the period, but as soon as the Territorial Defence started to be formed and transformed into the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I automatically joined the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that was a brief period and I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which armed unit were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Novi Grad Territorial Defence in Sarajevo and the Regional Defence Staff member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you join the 1st Corps at a certain point? Did you move to that unit?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. After that, I joined the 1st Corps immediately after it was established, because it was, in fact, the corps which was part of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you leave the 1st Corps at a certain point?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't leave it. I was transferred to a different post. I started working in 1993 as a chef de cabinet of the General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in relation to General Delic's appointment -- what position did General Delic hold at the time that you were appointed his Chief of Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly. That would be pure guesswork. I know that when he took over the duty of the Commander, immediately thereafter I think that I became the Chief of Cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And was General Delic your immediate superior while you were his Chief of Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where was General Delic's command post based when you became his Chief of Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, until it was relocated to the command post of Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And while you were his Chief of Cabinet, where were you -- where were you based?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sure. While you were General Delic's Chief of Cabinet, where were you based?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: At the command HQ. Do you want me to tell you the address, the street and the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No. I just want the city or the town.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you indicated that at a certain point, that the Command relocated to Kakanj. Were you a member of -- were you the Chief of Cabinet to General Delic when this happened?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when the command post in Kakanj was established, where were you based?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, what was the composition of General Delic's Cabinet in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: There were three of us, and I, as the Chief of Cabinet, the person who was in charge with -- of public relations, contact with the media, and there was a girl who was typing, a typist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And do you know the names of the other two people that you've referred to, the person in charge of public relations and the typist?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Zeljko Grubesic and Fatima -- I cannot remember her last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And let me clarify one of the answers that you had given. The command post in Kakanj, do you remember approximately when that was established?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I think that this was in late 1993 and early 1994. I can't remember the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when did -- how long did you remain the Chief of Cabinet to General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I think that I left the Commander's Cabinet in 1994. I cannot recall the exact time, but I did transfer to another duty, and there are exact orders on that, on the appointment, and you can check there. I think this was in early 1994. I don't know which month, but that's when I left the position of Chief of Cabinet and went to a different post also within the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, what were your duties as General Delic's Chief of Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: My duties mainly were to inform General Delic of all the documents that were arriving and that at some point to -- in some way to be in contact with the media, different structures, foreigners, political structures, make appointments with political structures. That was the work. Military/civilian structures, UNPROFOR, that was the extent of the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you -- that in your capacity as Chief of Cabinet, that you were responsible for informing General Delic of the documents that arrived. Can you describe how you went about transmitting these documents that arrived in the Cabinet for General Delic's attention?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: A large number of documents would arrive at the office, really a large number of documents, and I had to familiarise myself with the documents, make summaries of what the contents were, and then in brief, when the Commander had time, when I saw that he had time, I would go in and then inform him about the contents of the documents. That was the method of work that I applied when I was the Chief of Cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you describe how -- well, let me rephrase the question. The documents that General Delic signed, did he draft all of those documents?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Some of them, he did, but I also drafted some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And how would you go about drafting a document for General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: General Delic would summon me, and then he would tell me more or less what needed to be written in relation to specific matters. I would make notes and then draft the document, and then if I thought I would need to add something to be more precise in the document, I would do that, and then I would take it for his signature. If the General agreed, he would sign it. If not, he would make changes, he would tell me which changes would need to be made, and that's how the document was drafted. That's how I would draft the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And were you responsible for transmitting these documents to their intended recipient?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was responsible for dispatching it from the office. The documents would be dispatched via the Communication Centre or they would be sent by messenger. I would register the document. If it was my own document or if it was a document from the Cabinet, it would be registered, and after that it would be sent to the person it was addressed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you referred to the Communications Centre. Was the Communications Centre within the Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Where was the -- what was the relationship between the Communications Centre and the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: What do you mean what was the relationship?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: What was the function of the Communications Centre in relation to the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: The function of the Communications Centre was to send out the documents that were received via the Communications Centre, and there were specific or routine methods to send out these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. And beyond yourself, were there other organs or persons responsible for drafting documents for General Delic's signature?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you indicate who these other organs or persons were?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: They could have been Chiefs of Administration. They would write a document that would need to be signed by General Delic, and then the documents also would be sent for review and signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who were the -- in relation to the Chiefs of Administration, who is the immediate subordinate of the Chiefs of the Administrations? Excuse me, immediate superior of the Chiefs of the Administrations.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: They were subordinated to the Commander, from what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you say "the Commander," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Rasim Delic, General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what involvement did you have in ensuring that documents drafted by these administrations got to General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Most of the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you describe what your -- what your involvement was in ensuring that General Delic received these documents for his signature?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: The Chiefs of Administration would usually call the office and they would say that a document was coming, and then that the document would need to be signed. Then it would come to my desk, and I would take the document in for signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you describe what would happen after General Delic reviewed the document?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I would either call the person who drafted the document, and I would let them know that the document was signed and that they could come and pick it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in performing this function, did you -- did you witness General Delic signing documents?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't see it. I would just see that it was signed at the end, and I would call the person who signed the document and call them and say that the document was signed and that they could come and pick it up and that it was available for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And how many documents would you say that you saw which bore General Delic's signature in your time as his Chief of Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't say, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: There's no reason in particular. I saw a lot of signed documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did you become familiar with General Delic's signature?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you describe, Mr. Softic, what role you had, if any, in relation to meetings that General Delic would have in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Mostly, it had to do with scheduling meetings, summoning people to meetings, stating what the subject of the meeting was. I think that perhaps two or three times, I don't know, maybe once or twice, I attended meetings, but I really couldn't attend meetings because there was so much work to deal with, and people were coming and going. I really just had to make sure that the meeting proceeded well. There was always a lot to do in the -- in the Cabinet, a lot of things coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And with whom were you responsible for scheduling meetings, in terms of meetings with General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I know that there were mostly meetings with the Chiefs of Administrations, mostly with them. There were also meetings with corps commanders, but the corps commanders could rarely all attend and be there all together. There were meetings with the Commander of the 1st Corps, the Sarajevo Corps. I think mostly the meetings were with Chiefs of Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And were the Chiefs of Administrations contact you -- always contact you in order to meet with General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but perhaps it was also different. Perhaps in the way the meetings were scheduled directly, that the Chief of Administration perhaps would directly call General Delic, saying that he wanted to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you also refer to meetings with the corps commanders. Where did these meetings generally take place? Let me rephrase the question. When General Delic needed to meet the corps commanders, where would he generally have those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: In his office, from what I know, but again I say as far as the corps commanders were concerned, I think that he went into the field a lot and he met the corps commanders in the field. He wasn't able to convene meetings with corps commanders in Sarajevo because the situation was such and it dictated that things be done that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did the corps commanders have an obligation to submit written reports to the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Not the corps commanders. The Operations Centre, the Chief of Staff, actually, so the Operations Centre was the one that monitored the situation in the field, and the Operations Centre would receive reports from the corps. The Operations Centre, based on the reports from the corps, would draft a compiled report which was then forwarded to the Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who was responsible for the Operations Centre?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who was the Chief of Staff responsible to?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Softic. I would ask if the witness could be shown Exhibit P03068.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it P03068?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If you could have a quick look at this document, Mr. Softic. Can you please indicate to me -- for the record, can you please indicate what this document concerns?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the Supreme Command Staff of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that it was written by the Personnel Administration. Yes, Personnel Administration. And I can see that it's -- it bears the signature of General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you describe what the document provides for? In other words, what is the purpose of this document?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: It orders the -- or regulates the appointment of Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The appointment as what?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: The establishment post of Chief of Cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to direct your attention to the bottom left-hand corner of the document and to the initials "RM." Do you know who those initials would belong to?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I think that those are the initials of Rasim Mekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what position did Rasim Mekic hold in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: He did have a post. It was a post, but I don't recollect the exact title. He was in the Personnel Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And why would his initials appear on this document?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Because he drafted the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, again, just for the purpose of the record, could you indicate what the date of this document is?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: It's the 15th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, what do you wish the Chamber to extract from this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think this document, the relevance of this document, will become more apparent certainly as we go through the course of this witness's testimony, but other witnesses will comment upon the content of this document as well. And I'd be -- I'd be reluctant to comment upon the substance of the document or certainly the Prosecution's position on the document in front of this witness, especially in light of the other documents which I intend to show to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well, then. I hope it will be clear in our minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just be clear myself, you don't want it admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is one of the exhibits that was added pursuant to the Trial Chamber's decision, I believe, of the 7th of July to add new exhibits, and so there's a restriction in that decision which provides that exhibits -- the new exhibits may not be tendered into evidence before the 1st of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask if the witness could be shown Exhibit P01420.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, can you, for the purpose of the record, can you please just indicate what this document concerns?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I can read that it says: "Authorising Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin, a member of the 3rd Corps Command, to carry out, on behalf of the Commander of the RBH Armed Forces General Staff necessary negotiations and arguments with the representatives/commanders of the Mujahedin Unit from Zenica regarding the following issues." Should I repeat this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You referred -- in quoting from the document, you said "arguments." Are you sure that's what it says in the document? Can you read that line again?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: "Authorising Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin, member of the 3rd Corps Command, to carry out, on behalf of the Commander of the RBH Armed Forces General Staff negotiations necessary negotiations and arrangements with the representatives (commanders of the Mujahedin Unit from Zenica) regarding the following issues."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And can you just note for the record what the date of this document is?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: The 23rd of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I direct your attention to a set of digits underneath the heading of the document, and the digits are "1/297." Do you see those digits? They're on the left-hand -- upper left-hand side of the document.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you indicate whether these digits have any significance, and if so, what the significance is?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the numbers. These numbers could be the file number that I created, but I'm not sure. It's possible that that could be just a filing number when I was the Chief of Cabinet. The document -- actually, that's all I can say about the numbers. I'm not sure if this number is a number from the Commander's Cabinet, but I don't know. I'm not really sure. I can't -- I can't be certain. This would amount to guessing. I really don't know. It's been a long time. It could be from the Cabinet, and it doesn't necessarily have to be. It's very hard to say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Did the Cabinet have -- you referred to a filing number that you had when you were the Chief of Cabinet. Would this filing number be common -- be unique to the Cabinet of Rasim Delic, General Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. And can you look at the signature on the document? Does the signature resemble General Delic's signature?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: It does, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Softic. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness just responded, so I have no reason, but actually the question is strange. "Does it remind you of," or, "Does it resemble." I mean, that's a strange choice of words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But provided the strange words are objectionable. Now, they may be strange, but are they objectionable? Are you objecting, Madam Vidovic? And if you are, what is the basis for your objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do object, Your Honour. They could ask if it is or is not the signature in question, but they should not put the question in terms of, "Does it resemble the signature or not?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what is objectionable about saying "does it resemble"? I agree it's a very strange way of asking questions, but I don't see the objectionability of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will clarify this in the cross-examination with the witness. I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The signature that appears on the document, is that General Delic's signature, Mr. Softic, based upon your experience as his Chief of Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: The signature is a little bit strange, you know, I mean it's strange, because it looks like it was signed in haste, like it was done in haste, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Whether it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 271.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit P01461.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, can you for, the purpose of the record, could you just indicate what this document concerns?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: It concerns the document of the 3rd Corps, and it was forwarded to the Armed Forces Supreme Command Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it has to do with the establishment of a detachment by certain citizens. This is a proposal, rather. The Commander of the 3rd Corps proposes the establishment of some unit consisting of foreign citizens. That is the core of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who is the intended recipient of this document?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: The Staff of the Armed Forces Supreme Command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I'd like to draw your attention to a handwritten comment at the top of the document. It's in the middle at the top.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you indicate what that says?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: This comment is addressed to the Organisation and Mobilisation Administration by General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: And it says, further on, I agree --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And how do you know that this comment was made by General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I think this is his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I'd like to direct your attention to another comment, actually, and it's -- on the B/C/S version, it appears to be a "K," a dash, and then "DANT." Can you indicate what the significance of that comment might be, and it's also at the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: There's a -- at the top of the document, there's an indication of a date, a time, and then next to that there's a handwritten comment.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an original file, if that's what you're asking me about, and over here it says "Commander," "Commander" is what it says up here: "Commander --," original file, the source file, and document received by whoever it was received by through the Communication Centre, and up there it says "Commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: What's the significance of the reference to the Commander?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: This document is addressed to the Staff of the Supreme Command, that is to say, that the Supreme Command Staff would have to receive this document, which is to say not the Commander directly. But since it says "Commander" up here, well, I don't know how come. Somebody at the Communications Centre wrote this, "Commander," "Komandant." Now did this -- did the Commander get this directly through me or in some other way, I cannot recall, but it was supposed to go to the Staff of the Supreme Command, which is to say that the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command was supposed to be made aware of this document and then it was supposed to be forwarded to the Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And when you refer to the Commander, again just for the purpose of clarification, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you recognise General Delic's handwriting on this document. What would General Delic have done with this document after receiving it?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Well, this is one example. You see that he sent it to the Administration for Organisation and Mobilisation. He agrees with this document, with this proposal, and this Administration for Organisation and Mobilisation Affairs is duty-bound to further elaborate on the content of this document and to send it to him for his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 272.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P01466.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, for the sake of the record, could you indicate what the subject of this document is?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: This document is actually an order that has to do with the establishment of the El Mujahed Detachment in the 3rd Corps. It was sent to the Command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And for the sake of the record, could you indicate what the date of this document is?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: The 13th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who would be responsible for preparing this document for General Delic's signature?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Administration for Mobilisation and Organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And how would this document have reached General Delic from the Chief of Mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: It should have reached me in the Cabinet. Then I would briefly take a look and see what this was all about. I'd have to see what it was all about, and then after that I would give it to General Delic for his signature. That was the customary way of dealing with it. Perhaps other ways were used as well. Perhaps the Chief of the Administration could come directly and bring the document for signing in order to give some additional explanations. That is possible. There were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And the document is addressed to the 3rd Corps Command. How would this document have reached the 3rd Corps Command after General Delic signed it?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I assume that this document came through the Communications Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Softic. Your Honour, I would ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 273.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take note of the time. This would be a convenient point for me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You still have about three or four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. I will go to the next document, in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, could you -- excuse me. If the witness could be shown Exhibit P01576. And I've just been informed by my colleague that this exhibit has actually been -- this particular exhibit has been tendered into evidence and its number is 176. I will still be soliciting this witness's comments on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And why do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I recognise it by the heading, because it says "Cabinet of the Commander," and I realise that I created it because it has my initials at the bottom, "SM."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in preparing this document, what sources did you consult?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: It must have been another document which I cannot see here, on the basis of which I created the content of this document. That was what guided me in creating this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what other document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I say here "The President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, received a letter from special rapporteur for the former Yugoslavia, Mr. Tadeusz Mazowietcki --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Softic, please. The interpreter must catch up with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably a document existed on the basis of which I created this document, and I see that from the very beginning of this document of mine where it says: "The President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, received a letter from Mr. Tadeusz Mazowietcki, special rapporteur for the former Yugoslavia, containing claims about an alleged massacre of 25 Bosnian Croats (civilians) in the village of Maline on the 8th of July, 1993." So I'm not going to read any further. I had this document. On the basis of that document I created this document, probably at General Delic's orders, asking the Command of the 3rd Corps, because this happened in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, asking them to provide a more exhaustive report on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And just for the purpose of clarification, when you say "I had this document," can you indicate the author of the document to which you're referring? And let me clarify further. You had indicated, "I had this document. On the basis of that document, I created this document." If you could just clarify what document you're referring to that you used to create the document that's in front of you, and just indicate the author of the document that you consulted.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a document that was sent from the President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Who was the author of that document?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember. If you don't show me that document, I cannot -- I cannot say. But I see that I was referring to that document when I was creating this document, that document that probably came from the President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And after drafting this particular document, what did you do with it?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: General Delic probably ordered me to draft this document. I did draft this document, this document, yes, and I gave it to him to sign. The document was signed, and after that I see that the Communications Centre received it and sent it. That can be seen in the left-hand corner at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And did General Delic give you any instructions when you drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Well, he must have, but I cannot remember. But I think that the basis for this was that, well, he certainly instructed me to do that, ordered me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if I could just draw your attention to the upper left-hand side of the document, there's a strictly confidential number. Can you read out that number?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: "Strictly Confidential number 1/297-433."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The "1/297," does that number have any significance to you?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: When I look at it now, and I see it's the Cabinet, and I see that it's a document that came from the Cabinet of the Commander, this was the number of the Cabinet -- of the Commander, the number of the protocol, the number of that particular file. That was the basic reference number, and I think that this number, "433," was the number of the document under which this particular document was registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I asked you this in relation to another document that I showed you this morning, but the number "1297", would that have been specific to the Cabinet of Rasim Delic or unique to the Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I don't know what -- could you -- could you please show it to me again? I cannot recall the number that you showed me. I think it was the same one, but in order for me to be able to confirm this, you will have to show me the document again, the one that you're talking about right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon, would it perhaps be better to do that after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Menon. I think you've got about 35 minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, when we had left off, I was asking you a question about the strictly confidential number which appears on the upper left-hand side of this document. I'm going to, for the purpose of clarification, I'm just going to ask you this question again. If you could direct your attention to the digits "1/297", what was the purpose of that number on this document?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: That is the reference number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The number --

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: The basic number of the document, that is, of the Cabinet of the Commander. I don't know whether this number pertains specifically to the Cabinet of the Commander because -- I assume it did, because it says; "Cabinet of the Commander," which means that "1/297" was the number of the file of the Cabinet of the Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would ask that this document be tendered into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this not the document that you said is already Exhibit 176?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I apologise for that. Could I have a minute to consult with my case manager on the next document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And before I show the witness the next document that I'd like to have him authenticate, I'd just like to go back to a document I showed him earlier today, and it's been admitted into evidence as Exhibit number 271. If that could be shown to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, could you -- and I'm going to refer you to the digits that are next to the reference "Conf number," there's a set of four digits that goes "1/297". Can you indicate what the significance of those numbers may have been based upon the other documents that you've seen?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: This number, "1/297," is identical. It is the same number that I saw on the document previously shown, that is to say, that this number belonged to the Cabinet of the Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 231.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we find that next document, Counsel, apart from asserting that the archive number, 1/297, shows that it belongs to the Cabinet of the Commander, I'd like to ask the witness if he recalls what was in that case file number 297. In particular, would this number refer to correspondence relating to the Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, you've heard the Judge's question, have you not? Do you understand the Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: This number probably did not include the entire correspondence related to the Mujahedin; that is to say that, in this number one could find only that correspondence related to the Mujahedin that had come to the Cabinet of the Commander and to which the Commander replied, that is to say, only the correspondence that reached the Cabinet of the Commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Softic, did the number 297 have a name? I suppose it refers to a case file. Did that file have a name? What was the heading of the case file numbered 1/297, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was not a case file. This file consisted of documents that left the Cabinet of the Commander, and those documents that were addressed to the Commander and that had come to the Cabinet of the Commander and that he was able to identify, those were the documents contained in that file; that is to say, outgoing documents and incoming documents signed by the -- incoming mail addressed to the Cabinet of the Commander and outgoing mail signed by the Commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you these questions because apparently the Prosecution has put some weight to it, and I want to understand the reason why. So let me ask you just one more question. Building up an archive is a very complicated issue, is a very difficult thing to do, and the number 1/297 dash something else, was that part of a number that was designed by you to serve as the archive for the Commander or was it a number that belonged to an archive system that had been created for all parts of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was not an invented number. I, as Chief of Cabinet, received this number, so this number had been recorded, and I used this as a number that had been received. I don't know how it was that these numbers were assigned, but I was told specifically about this one, 1/297, that this is the number of the Cabinet of the Commander for one period. These numbers would change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Softic. I assume that the Prosecution will provide some more clarity about the significance of the reference numbers here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, the number 54, can you explain what the -- actually, if we could go back to the exhibit that we were discussing. That would be Exhibit 272. Excuse me, 271, it's 271. And I just want to direct you to the digits that we were discussing. After the "1/297," there's a digit -- there's the number "54." Can you explain what the significance of that number would be?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, 1/297 is the basic reference number, the reference number, whereas 54 pertains specifically to this document. This document is numbered 54, and that is how this particular document was filed in my file, registered in my file.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If the witness now could be --

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: That is what it should mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit 231.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, if you could look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Could you please enlarge this a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to familiarise yourself with this document, Mr. Softic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Certainly, because this had come to the Cabinet of the Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would just ask that the witness now be shown Exhibit 178.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon, this is exhibit what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: 178, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're done with 231?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I just wanted the witness to see it and to familiarise himself with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, if you could look at this document and familiarise yourself with it. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Can you please scroll it down a bit? I can't see the whole document in the Bosnian version. I need to see the end of the document. I would like to see the initials of the person who drafted this document. Can you show that to me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And for the record, that would be at the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, now I can see it, and this document was drafted by me, probably following an order from General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And what does this document concern?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Can I have the document back, please, again? This -- the contents of this document refers to -- it's a response to Mr. Mazowiecki's request relating to the conduct of certain foreign -- or rather his request -- Mr. Mazowiecki's request, and that's the response to his request. I think I've seen this document before, and I believe that this was given to the foreign ministry in order to provide a response to Mr. Mazowiecki in response to his request for clarification of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you indicated that you were responsible for drafting the document. How would you have gone about drafting this document?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I must have written this document, and I've seen the document that you showed me earlier, received from the 3rd Corps Command. We wrote to the 3rd Corps Command on the order of General Delic, asking them to give us precise information about what had happened on the ground. Once I received a report from the 3rd Corps, on the basis of that report, I drafted this report and sent it to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in order to convey this to Mr. Mazowiecki.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: After drafting the document, what did you do with this document?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I followed the standard procedure. It was signed and then it was submitted. Whether it was sent by courier or through the Communications Centre, I couldn't tell. Either by a courier or through the Communications Centre, I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Did General Delic give you any instructions when drafting this document?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I think that the focus was the source from the 3rd Corps, probably had General Delic had some objections, he would have made them to me, because without his signature, this document could not leave the office. He probably ordered me to draft this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm done with this document, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Exhibit P01661.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And would you, in your capacity as General Delic's Chief of Cabinet, would you receive such documents?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I would receive them from the Operations Centre, not directly from the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. And for the sake of the record, I'd like to direct your attention, and this is -- and I'd like to refer to page 1 of the B/C/S copy of this document and page 2 of the English version of this document, and it's to the second paragraph under the heading 2.2 "Our Forces." If you could just read that paragraph out to us, the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: "In the zone of responsibility of the 325th" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It's the second paragraph that I'm interested in, the second paragraph under the heading 2.2.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: "314th Brigade and the Technical Group" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we cannot locate this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Neither can the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It's the second paragraph under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the second paragraph under heading 2.2 starts with the words: "In the general, tt-511 area" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'm mistaken. I'm referring to the paragraph where there was a separation between the text under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 3rd and 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Exactly. That's the one. I took that to be the second paragraph because of the separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, if you could read the section that you just read out to me again.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Only now I can see: "The 3rd and the 4th Battalions of the 17th SKbbr and the South Tactical Group, the 1st Battalion of the 7th Motorised Brigade, and the El Mujahedin Detachment, put off the continuation of combat operations until tomorrow due to continuing reconnaissance activity." And it goes on to list the casualties sustained so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if I could refer you to the top of this document on the first page, can you note the date of the document for the record?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I cannot see clearly. There are some numbers over it. I cannot see the date. Can you stop for a second? It's the 24th of October or December, I don't know, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page of the document -- or the second-to-last page of the document in the B/C/S and the last page of the document in the English version. If you could just note for the record, who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I cannot recognise this signature, but it says here "Commander Alagic." I'm not familiar with this signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But do you know what position General or Commander Alagic, as it states in the document, had in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: He was a corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I would ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 274.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, you indicated that you left the office of General Delic's Cabinet, and I believe if memory serves me correct, that it was at the end of 1993 or the beginning of 1994. Who succeeded you in that position?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: His first name was Ferid, but I can't remember his last name. He was the person who replaced me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And who replaced the gentleman that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Ferid Buljubasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And where did you go after you left the Cabinet of General Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I went to the Intelligence Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any cross-examination, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours. Your Honours, I would like to emphasise that this witness has knowledge which is of importance for the Defence case of General Delic, and we are also going to ask certain questions with respect to that. Cross-examination by Madam Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Softic.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and I'm going to examine you on behalf of the Defence team for General Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please switch off the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You told us that you were appointed Chief of Cabinet of the Supreme Command immediately upon the arrival of General Delic. This duty of Mr. Delic's Chief of Cabinet during 1993 was not discharged by Sakib Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: In early 1993, he was actually in the Cabinet of Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: In the spring of 1993, he went to Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: During your work in the Cabinet, you told us that the Cabinet was made up of only three persons; yourself, Mr. Zeljko Grubesic, and a typist?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Grubesic was one of the first associates of General Delic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: He worked in his Cabinet throughout the whole war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I apologise. Since we speak the same language, we need to pause between questions and answers. Now, I will go back to Mr. Grubesic. Zeljko Grubesic was a Bosnian Croat; right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The Commander of the Supreme Command Staff was a newly-established post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Before that, there was no such post in the establishment of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic was the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command rather than a commander; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: In that sense, I thought that there was no Commander of the Staff of the Supreme Command but rather a Chief of the Staff of the Supreme Command. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Therefore, the function of the Commander of the Supreme Command was only introduced on the 8th of June, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: When you came to work in the Cabinet, there were no set of rules governing the operation of the Cabinet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I didn't find any such set of rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You wanted to write these rules, but due to the work-load, you never found time to do that?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Primarily because of the work-load and also I couldn't receive proper instructions, but first of all due to an enormous workload.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Throughout the whole period that you worked as a chief of cabinet of Mr. Delic, that is to say, the latter half of 1993 and first month of 1994, when you left it, Mr. Delic's Cabinet was practically in the process of being established; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, one may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You do remember that you made a statement to the Prosecution in this case?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I refer now to paragraph 54 of this statement, in which you said everything during that time was subject to changes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: For that reason and due to these changes and the lack of organisation of the Cabinet, would you agree with me that you were working under difficult conditions?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, under very difficult conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The work-load was enormous, and there were only three of you?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.
