utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You personally had a whole range of duties?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You set up meetings for General Delic when he was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You prepared these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Most of the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You mediated between the administrations and General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, in most cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You did not attend the meetings between General Delic and the Chiefs of Administration?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: For the most part, no, because there was a lot of pressure on the Cabinet, and we had other duties to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: In your testimony today, in response to the Prosecutor's questions regarding the administrations, you said, if I understood you correctly, that the administrations were directly linked to the Commander of the Staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the Operations Centre, the Intelligence Administration, the Administration for Organisation and Mobilisation, the Administration of Branches, and the PV and RM Administration - I don't know what it stands exactly for - were directly linked to the Chief of the Supreme Command Staff; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Operations Centre was directly linked. Which other did you mention?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Intelligence Administration, the Administration for Organisation and Mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: The Organisation and Mobilisation Administration --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If you can remember, fine. If you cannot --

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chiefs of Administrations had their subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Their subordinates briefed them about the problems and the developments?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: There was a hierarchy between administrations of the Supreme Command and appropriate departments of these administrations in lower-ranking units?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: For example, the Chief of the Administration for Moral Guidance of the Supreme Command received reports from the corps organs for moral guidance?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Such subordination existed in the Military Service as well?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: These administrations of the Supreme Command Staff had their own protocols or registers where the documents were entered that were received or dispatched from those administrations?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Documents that were received by the administrations from the field did not have to be seen at the Cabinet of General Delic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Also, documents that were sent by certain Supreme Command Staff administrations into the field were not something that the Cabinet of General Delic had to see; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: They didn't even have to hear about them?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The chief of the relevant administration of the Supreme Command Staff, when he received information from their subordinates from the field, would decide about the importance or the significance of the problem?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: He would decide whether or not that is something that they would inform the Supreme Command Staff Commander or not?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, depending on the content of the document, he would decide whether he would inform the Commander or not; specifically, General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Only if he felt, and I'm thinking of the administration chief, that it was an important piece of information, it would reach the Supreme Command Staff Commander; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are. If the administration chief felt that the information was important at that level of command, that the Commander needed to know about it, then it would be passed on to the Commander. In other words, if he made a different assessment, it would not reach the Commander?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It all depended on his estimate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it all depended on his assessment of the content of a specific piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You would agree that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina was difficult; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It was difficult to members of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The forces of the BiH Army practically controlled five separate enclaves where the population that was loyal to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was herded and parts of Central Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The communication was very difficult, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The Command in Sarajevo was isolated to a large degree; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Its information about events and the situation depended on the information that was arriving from the field; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Information did not always reflect the actual situation in the field; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And that is why General Delic, whenever he could, toured the units; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And he did this whenever the combat situation allowed, which was actually pretty intense, so depending on the combat actions, which were very intense around Sarajevo throughout the war, he did it when this was possible?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: In the second half of 1993, there were internal settling -- there was internal settling of accounts within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina with units of the 1st Corps that had gone out of control of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You will agree that this made the situation and the conditions of the work of the Command more difficult?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You testified about the mail and the documents that arrived at the Cabinet and were dispatched from the Cabinet. The mail that came to the Cabinet was addressed to the Cabinet or, rather, to the Commander personally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Commander Delic faced a large number of problems because of the difficult combat situation for the armija in Sarajevo and outside; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Because of the large number of problems, the Cabinet was absolutely overwhelmed by mail; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: When you testified or when you gave your statement to the Prosecutor before this trial, and we're talking about paragraph 41, you said: "I was the one who filtered or channeled the mail." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The contents and the importance of the situation was something that you were guided by in terms of which information you would pass on to the Commander or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The importance of a document, in your assessment, would then set the priorities as far as the documents that the Commander would see were concerned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You couldn't show all the documents to the Commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You passed the documents directly on to the administrations if you felt that the administrations could resolve the problem without the involvement of the Commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Because they had their Chiefs?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: So even though the document would come to the Cabinet of the Commander, if I saw that the chief of the relevant administration could resolve the problem, then I would forward it to the particular administration chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. In the absence of the Commander, you would resolve the problems with his deputies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: These were Generals Stjepan Siber and General Jovan Divjak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: General Delic trusted his deputies, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I think that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And then you would turn to them in his absence?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: In providing your statement to the Prosecutor, in paragraph 47 of the statement you said: "He told me," meaning General Delic, "you have Siber and Divjak here and you could resolve things in my an absence"?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: So there was a protocol on who would stand in for him?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly, but I think that there must have been a decision on who would stand in for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: All right. But most frequently General Siber would stand in for him; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You worked with General Delic from the time you were appointed until sometime, as you said, in early 1994. During this period, did he ever tell you that you could not discuss any information or any particular problem with his deputy?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: No, he never told me anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: He didn't tell you that you could not resolve any particular question with his deputy?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: No, he never said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness please look at document D238. For the transcript, this is a Supreme Command Staff document, implementation of an order of the 19th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Witness, please, can you look at this document? You can see the date. It's the 19th of September, 1993. And then I think that your initials are here, "SM/AM." Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's my document, it's a document from the Cabinet of the Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you please look where it says "for the Commander, Mr. Stjepan Siber." Do you recognise his signature?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I think that is Siber's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now I'm going to quote the middle part of the document. Your Honours, it's paragraph 2 of the document, which states -- Siber is asking for the order to be implemented and states: "One such vehicle was taken on the 15th of August, 1993, as the UNPROFOR document states, by the Mujahedin near Celebici, 2-3 kilometres from Celebici. Detailed information regarding this case is provided in the above-mentioned order." Now, in relation to this document, I would like to ask you: This document shows, does it not, that General Siber resolved certain problems in relation to the Mujahedin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's his signature. I think it's his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: These problems were not concealed from him, were they?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I didn't conceal anything when I would come up against a problem and I had to resolve it. I didn't have anyone else to go to, and it was my duty to go to the Deputy Commander and, in that way, resolve my own problem and the problem that was imposed on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You didn't have any instructions to put anything to the side as far as the Mujahedin were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: No, never. There was nothing like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 275.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I would like to ask you the following: It's correct, isn't it, that Supreme Command Staff documents were archived, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The archives were equally accessible to the Deputy Commanders and to the Commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that deputies did have access to the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And to look at whatever document they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I meant when I said that was that they could go to the archive, and they could ask for whatever they wanted in the archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The Main Staff did not have any secret archives, did it?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You never archived a document in a separate archive or safe, and that this was not part of the normal Supreme Command Staff archive?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Would you agree that members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, during 1993, knew little about what an important security-related piece of information was?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. If I were to talk about that, it would take up a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Many documents were classified as confidential or strictly confidential, when this was actually not the case?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You showed the Commander these documents if they really contained important and significant information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: This also applied to the bulletin and special information or reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You showed the Commander these documents if they really contained what they believed to be strategically-important information that the Commander had to know?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you something about processing the documents that were received or sent out by the Supreme Command Staff Commander or his Cabinet, and this is something that you also were asked by the Prosecutor. Would you agree that the Cabinet had a protocol where incoming and outgoing mail was registered?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The incoming document would be given a protocol number; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to clarify. May I? A document that was received would be given a protocol number, but a document that was received also had its own reference number and it would state the person who had sent it, and it would have its own reference number. I would register the contents of the documents in a separate column. Then I would note where the document came from, summary contents of the document, and also the date when it was received, and also then I would give it a number under which I had entered it in my own register.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you helped all of us with this exhaustive information or explanation. I would like to ask you the following: It was not possible for a document to have a protocol number without being entered into the protocol precisely under that number; do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: A document would have the number "1297/54," and if this number was not found in the protocol it would just mean that the protocol -- the document was not entered into the protocol?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: That is something that should not have been allowed to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to come back to these documents that the Prosecutor showed you, and I will put some more questions about that to you, but now I would like for us to look at another document, D247 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, D246.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document of the Supreme Command Staff of the 29th of June, 1993. Can we please scroll down the document so we can see the signature, or, rather, can we look at page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you agree that that is a document that was signed by General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the document be returned to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I kindly ask you to look at paragraph 1 first. It says: "An Operations Centre is to be formed at the Supreme Command Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for constant monitoring and estimating of the b/d/combat operations in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and so on." Could you please look at number 3 now: "The Operations Centre of the SVK is directly subordinated to the Chief of Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And that is the 29th of June, 1993. Do you agree that in actual fact that is how things worked in practice as well?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The documents arrived in the Operations Centre, right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The Operations Centre, as we can see, was subordinated to the Chief of Staff, so information was submitted to the Chief of Staff then; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: All documents that arrived in the Operations Centre had to be presented to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: At this time, the 29th of June, 1993, you will agree it was Sefer Halilovic; right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: After that the Chief of Staff decided on how important the document was and whether it was necessary to show it to the Commander of the Main Staff; is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: That is certainly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, could this document please be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we do that, just reading that paragraph three: "The Operations Centre of the SVK is subordinated directly to the Army of RBiH Chief of Staff," and your reading the B/C/S version of it, doesn't have -- that word, "potcinjen," doesn't seem to have the "pret" that we had earlier referred to "re-subordination." So it does look like there is a distinction between subordination and re-subordination. Can we agree with that? In an earlier document, where the word in English was "re-subordination," that "potcinjen" had a prefix before it. So it is not correct to say that in the B/C/S "subordination" and "re-subordination" have one word.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, but when someone comes -- well, I don't know whether the witness can help us with this, but there will be witnesses who will know exactly what "re-subordination" means in our language, "pret potcinjen." In our language it comes from the word "pret potjcinjen," which is "re-subordinated." So it's "re-subordination" and "re-subordinated." We have the next witnesses that will be coming in and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think we need a witness to explain this to us. The documents speak for themselves. We have here the word "subordinate" and we have this word here which doesn't "pret," and earlier when we had "re-subordinate," this word was prefixed by "pret." That's all I'm saying. And I don't think we need any witness to explain this because the document, I think, speak for themselves. I just wanted to make that note. Having made that note, the document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Exhibit number 276.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Certainly, we are going to deal with this question that you drew our attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, please, D244 is the document that I would like to have shown to the witness. Witness, this is a document of the 3rd Corps dated the 9th of August, 1993, and you see that it is called a combat report?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: A regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: A regular combat report addressed to the SVK. Now, please, see this part here: "Mujahedin or Muslim forces that were brought from Travnik, as well as part of the Muslim forces from Zavidovici ..." It's around the middle of the document in the English language, Your Honours. "Part of the Muslim forces from Zavidovici not want to carry out an order." Please, do you agree that this is a report that arrived from the field to the Staff of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, could this document please be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 277.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now see D235.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that this is a document that is a report addressed to the President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Could you just scroll down so that we see the signature? And in relation to this, I ask you to look at paragraphs 6 and 7 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: You mean the last one and the one-but-last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Not quite.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You see where Muslim forces are referred to? Could the English text please be scrolled down so that the Trial Chamber can see? And then it continues on the other page in English. Witness, do you see that this document bears the initials "HP/MP"?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you agree -- or, rather, who is "HP"; can you tell us, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Is it possible there was someone who did --

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the Operations Centre. That can be seen from the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Husa Paravlic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, Husa Paravlic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you agree that over here General Delic informs the President of the Presidency that the Muslim forces brought from Travnik and from Zavidovici refuse to carry out an order, and as a reason they mention that they do not trust the army and that they fear treason?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you agree that here, for instance, the Operations Centre estimated that this was an important security problem and informed Delic about this?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And then Delic informed the President of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Because this was an important security problem in the field, the assessment was that the document should reach Delic, and then from Delic, the President of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this was indeed a problem that merited such a development.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Because what is pointed out is they do not trust the army, and they fear treason, right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is what was said, that they do not trust the army and that they fear treason.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, could this document please be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 278.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the break I think that the witness can have a look at another document that will require very little time, Exhibit number 225. Could that please be shown to the witness. For the transcript this is a document of the Supreme Command Staff of the 27th of July, 1993, and it is entitled "Warning."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: So witness, please, it doesn't seem to be right -- could you please adjust the Bosnian version of the document a bit? Just look at the last part of the document, where it says -- or rather the document refers to the establishment of Muslim armed forces, units within them, and about them becoming independent and so on, so just look at this document: "Take all necessary measures to prevent these and other activities in the breaking of that unity, and to bring armed formations under the single system of command and control. Please, do you agree that this document reflects the position of General Delic vis a vis the Muslim armed forces? Quite simply, he ordered a ban on the activity of the Muslim armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes. What is written here in this document reflects the position of General Delic. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: He sent this document to all the corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes. That can be seen in the heading on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, this exhibit has a number, so can it please be removed now. Your Honours, perhaps this would be a convenient moment for the break, because as far as the next document is concerned, I will have more questions. But if you wish ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then as you may, we'll take a break now and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, the Prosecutor has shown you a document on the 3rd Corps relating to the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment, dating 12th --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please repeat the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Counsel, you are requested to repeat the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: ... dated 12th of August, 1993, Exhibit 273. Witness, can you please look at this document. Would you agree that under item 1, the formation of the detachment, it reads: "In the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, El Mujahedin Detachment shall be formed according to the proposed establishment, which you must submit to this Staff for approval." Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you agree that, in principle, the Administration for Organisation and Mobilisation of the Staff of the Supreme Command should give an establishment formation to the unit formed under the order of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, based on the proposal of this subordinate unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Therefore, that would be a standard and normal procedure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: This order for the formation says that the 3rd Corps will form this detachment according to the proposed establishment which itself has to submit to the Staff?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, based on the proposal of the 3rd Corps in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: This means that the Supreme Command Staff was not aware of the elements on the basis of which it could immediately order the formation of the detachment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It was up to the 3rd Corps to provide elements on the basis of which all this would be formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Very well. Therefore, it should contain the potential to form the unit both in terms of men and materiel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: While you were the Chief of Cabinet of General Delic, he did not receive this proposal for this formation; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember receiving this proposal. I definitely don't remember receiving it. I would have to see it to refresh my memory. I don't remember receiving it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can the witness now be shown the next page of this document. Would you please look at item 5 of the document, which reads: "Submit a written report on the implementation of this order to this Staff no later than the 5th September 1993."

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Please, while you were working in the Cabinet of General Staff, have you ever seen such a report?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I honestly cannot remember seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Would that be something very special that would be remembered and noticed by you?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I should have noticed such a thing, I should have done that, because that would be an important matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, can we just scroll down this document, or, rather, up? Yes, that would be it. Very well. Your Honours, I think that this document can be removed from the screens. I was trying to match the translation, but I can do it some other time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Can the witness be shown Exhibit number 271, please. It's a letter dated 23rd of July, 1993, and that's an authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Witness, can you please look carefully once again at the substance of this document. First of all, do you agree that it's dated the 23rd of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And there are no initials of yours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I usually or normally put my initials on every document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, please look carefully at this document. It is true, isn't it, that this document has no incoming or outcoming stamp on the face of it?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I don't see that this document was sent out anywhere. If you can scroll it up because normally the Communications Centre would mark it. But I don't see any such mark here that I would normally see, which means that this was not dispatched anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Very well. You were well aware of the way and style of General Delic's writing?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: You can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Please, General Delic was an educated officer, he had completed the Staff Command School; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Would he issue an order to a subordinate of his or would he draft an authorisation?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat this or rephrase it more accurately?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Please, General Delic, as a well-educated officer, would issue an order to a subordinate of his?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: However, being an officer yourself, is there such a term as "authorisation" in military terminology?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: This is not how things should be done, how you would write to a subordinate unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Please, it also says here "authorising Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin, a member of the 3rd Corps." Would you agree that a military order issued by a trained officer, such as Delic, would be given to Sakib Mahmuljin and to state his --

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether his post would be mentioned, but it shouldn't [as interpreted] be mentioned; that is to say, the post of Sakib Mahmuljin. That is correct, it should contain the post held by Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you agree that this kind of letter, provided that it was dispatched somewhere, must have been entered into the register book of the office?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And it would be given a number?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You can see here that the member of the 3rd Corps Command is given an authorisation. You would agree with that. If this letter was sent to the 3rd Corps, it must have been entered in the protocol of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, with respect to this document, I would like the witness to look again at the MFI 270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we do so, Counsel, you have suggested that it would be unusual for General Delic to authorise the Chef de Cabinet of the 3rd Corps to carry out, on behalf of a supreme authority, arrangements relating to the Mujahedin. I understand your answer to the counsel's question as saying that under normal circumstances General Delic would have ordered not the Chef de Cabinet, but the Chief of the 3rd Corps directly, to do these things. So in the answer and questions that went on between you and counsel, I got the impression that there is something strange about this document. Why would General Delic authorise rather than ordering these things to be done, and why would he address himself to the Chef de Cabinet rather than to the Chief? Do we have any explanations as to why this was done the way it was here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I understood you correctly, General Delic would never address the Cabinet of the 3rd Corps Command. He did communicate with the Commander of the 3rd Corps, and I think that this is how it was done, and the 3rd Corps Commander was subordinated to General Delic. I cannot understand your objection and your remark. I think that this line of communication was clear. However, as far as this specific document is concerned, I can only say that I don't see that this document was forwarded to any quarters, nor is this, as far as I can judge, the style of writing of General Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And that is exactly what puzzles me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me. And that is exactly why I am puzzled, because -- and I'm not raising an objection, not at all. This is not my function, but I'm merely putting a question. Because it seems to me that it is strange that General Delic would authorise Mr. Mahmuljin, who I understand was the Chef de Cabinet for General Hadzihasanovic. Why would he authorise Mr. Mahmuljin to ensure this inclusion of the Mujahedin Unit into the RBiH Army? That is clearly not something that would fall under the authority of the Chef de Cabinet. That would fall under the authority of the Commander of the 3rd Corps, General Hadzihasanovic. So there's a bell that rings inside my head that this is strange somehow, and I'm asking you if you can provide some explanation to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honour, I don't know whether Sakib Mahmuljin was the Chief of Cabinet of the 3rd Corps Commander. I'm not aware of that to begin with. Secondly, I know only one thing. Technically speaking, if a commander addressed the 3rd Corps, he would communicate with the 3rd Corps Commander. The Cabinet can only act as a technical liaison between General Delic and the 3rd Corps Commander and under no other circumstances can this be done otherwise. I don't know what Sakib Mahmuljin was doing, whether he was the Chief of Cabinet, what post he held. I truly don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Softic. I thought that this was your own testimony from -- right from the beginning of your testimony today. Exhibit 270, 270, I think authorised Mahmuljin as the Chef de Cabinet, I think, or maybe I was wrong. If we can see Exhibit 270 again or come back to it later.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I may be confused, Mr. Softic. I'm sorry. I thought that Mahmuljin had been appointed the Chef de Cabinet, but I must have been wrong. I realise that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was precisely my intention, for us to look at the MFI 270, and that was my plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have questions on this one before we remove this one. It was suggested to you, sir, that this document was not sent anywhere, not dispatched anywhere. Amongst others, one of the reasons given is that it does not have a number. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this the previous document I have in front of me a different document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, this one, "Authorisation."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Authorisation." No, you cannot say that, Your Honour, on the basis of this number. It can be said, on the basis of the fact that there is no stamp at the bottom or at the top of the document, that the document was forwarded. This is a document that should have been sent to the 3rd Corps. Such documents were dispatched via the Operations Staff Communications Centre, and when they would forward such a document, it would have to have proof on the document that it actually was forwarded to the 3rd Corps. And this is why I said that it probably was not forwarded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get an understanding. At page 70, line 9, it was said to you: "Do you agree that this kind of letter, provided that it was dispatched somewhere, must have been entered into the register book of the office?" And you said: "Yes." Now, how do we know now, by looking at this document, that it was not entered into the register of the office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This seems to be a document that was registered, because at the top of the document we have the number "1/297-54," which means that the document was entered on the 23rd of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's take it step by step. Don't go ahead of me. I'm asking you the question. It was said to you: "Do you agree that this kind of letter, provided that it was dispatched somewhere, must have been entered into the register book of the office." And you said: "Yes." I'm asking you a very simple question. How do you determine, by looking at this document, that it was not entered in the register?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document was entered into the protocol in File 1/297 under number 57.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 54, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then -- but then the next question was: "And it would be given a number," and you said: "Yes," the suggestion being this one does not have a number. Now you're telling us that the number is 54?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So when you said, "Yes," to the question, "And you'd be given a number," were you not correct? I'm trying to understand this discussion now, because I didn't understand how it was going.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the Defence counsel asked a general question, how this is done, what the procedure is in processing documents. Had she asked me specifically about this document, I would have given her an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: These questions were put to you after this document was put on the screen, and we are under the impression that we are talking about this document. And this document has a number, but then it has been suggested that it would have a number if it was dispatched somewhere, and because the position is that it was not dispatched somewhere, therefore, it doesn't have a number and it is not entered into the register. And I'm asking you these two questions: How do we find out, by looking at the document, that it was entered into the register, and does it have a number? Now, you've answered that it does have a number. And if I may ask you again something that you, yourself, have said. You said it would have a stamp. What kind of stamp would be there to say that it has been dispatched, because this one here does have a stamp over the signature of the author. I don't know what the stamp means, but there is some stamp there. What other stamp is it supposed to have to demonstrate that it has been dispatched? We can go to other documents. Let's see what other documents have -- what stamp they have which this one doesn't have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a stamp of the Supreme Command Staff. Usually, what would happen is that the Commander, when he signed a document, next to the signature, even in haste it would be done on top of his signature, this stamp would be applied. That was the usual manner, the usual procedure. After the document was created, this would then constitute the final step in sending a document off, the signature of General Delic and the stamp of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but am I right to say -- I don't want to misinterpret you. Am I right to say that you did indicate earlier that amongst other things to indicate that the document was dispatched, it's got to have a stamp, a particular type of stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. In order to send a document, I didn't say that it had to have a stamp in order to dispatch a document. I knew that the document was sent on the basis of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, finish off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a major difference between the stamp --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read what was said at page 69, starting at lines 7 to 10: "I don't see that this document was sent out anywhere." This is your answer: "If you can scroll it up, because normally the Communications Centre would mark it, but I don't see any mark here which I would normally see, which means that this was not dispatched anywhere." Now, you are talking specifically about this document. You are telling us specifically that this document was not dispatched anywhere because you don't see the mark. What kind of mark would have been on this document to demonstrate that it was dispatched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if -- when a document reached the Communications Centre and when the document was dispatched, the person who dispatched the particular document at the Communications Centre, and the document would be dispatched via radio equipment, the usual procedure was to make a brief note, a brief remark, that the document was sent off, the time when it was sent off, and there would be an initial next to it. That would be at the end of the document. And this is why I asserted that the document was never dispatched anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Judge Lattanzi has a question, and after that I would like us to be shown another document which has those marks from the Communications Centre, a document that was dispatched. Yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, is it possible that this particular document does not bear the markings you're mentioning for the simple reason that the Tribunal received this document directly from the Supreme Command rather than from the Communications Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document, regardless of where it was taken from in its original version, must have this note. Anywhere the document would be received at, it would have to have that mark. It doesn't matter where the document was obtained from, where the Court got the document from. The original of the document would have such a mark. Even the photocopy, such as this one, would still have to bear this particular mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, you have said you wanted to show the witness the next document. We'll look at that document and look out for the marks. Can you call the document you want to call.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honours, can we look at the document that we just looked at a little bit earlier? This is Exhibit 273. This is a document signed by General Delic on the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment. We looked at this earlier. It's also sent to the 3rd Corps Command. This is Exhibit 273. Can you scroll down the page, please, a little bit more, so that you could see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Witness, please, can you look at this document again? This note, that the document was dispatched or delivered, is something that is handwritten, "CVSVKOSKZP," so it's encrypted, sent to the 3rd Corps on the 14th of August, 1993, at 1630 hours, signed Hari, the person who dispatched it. Is that what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was talking about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, can we now please look at -- Your Honours, do you have any more questions on this, or can I continue with my next exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If you could go back to Exhibit 270, which I thought you said that you would come back to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour. This is what I was going to do. This is MFI 270. MFI -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Witness, you answered questions from the Prosecutor about this document, and this is a document appointing Sakib Mahmuljin as Chief of Cabinet of the Supreme Command Staff, and the document is dated the 15th of June, 1993. My question is about what Sakib Mahmuljin was doing in early 1993. In response to my question, you said he was in Sefer Halilovic's Cabinet. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that he was in Sefer Halilovic's Cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And that after that, he went to Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that after that he went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Please, he never worked on duties during the time that you were there in 1993, Sakib Mahmuljin never performed these duties?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: What is more -- at that time, in that period, he was not in Sarajevo at all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that -- he was not in Sarajevo at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you see here the date, the 15th of June, 1993, whereby Sakib Mahmuljin was supposed to be appointed to the establishment post of Chief of Cabinet? Earlier, we saw this authorisation of the 23rd of June that we are discussing or that we were discussing. Do you agree? Do you recall that, in the document created less than a month or three weeks after this document, that it said in that authorisation that Sakib Mahmuljin was a member of the 3rd Corps Command; do you recall the document stating that?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Please, if, on the 23rd of July, General Delic wrote that document, and if this document here is correct, that he is his Chief of Cabinet, he would not then address him as a member of the 3rd Corps Command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you agree that there is something wrong with either of these documents or with both of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I didn't see this document. Had I seen it before, perhaps I would have reacted to this document first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can we clarify one more thing that we discussed a little bit earlier, please? An authorisation -- or any document that has a specific number, if we want to check whether that document is authentic and whether it's registered under that same number, we would be able to see that in the protocol logbook; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: In the same way, if a document was sent to the 3rd Corps, it couldn't just fly through the air. It would be recorded in the protocol logbook of the 3rd Corps; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would have to be logged in the protocol book of the 3rd Corps Command, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, perhaps these documents can be put away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just see the bottom of the documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, you said yourself that there was something wrong with these documents, but I never understood what was wrong, and I still have the question of why would General Delic deal with the matter of integrating the Mujahedin into the 3rd Corps with anyone else but the Commander, himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is addressed to me? I think that the communication should have been with the Commander, himself, and probably General Delic should have communicated, and he probably did, I assume, with the Commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you do not have any -- so do you have any recollection of why an authorisation to Mahmuljin was made? If you don't have it, then that's fine, just say so. Then we will drop it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The nature of this document is not clear to me, "Authorisation," why it's done like that, who drafted it. It's not clear to me. Many things about this document are not clear to me. It was not logical. The contents -- from the contents, I think it's a very brief document, not written in a military manner, not dispatched. Many things about this document are not clear. I really cannot recall, Your Honour, the contents. I mean, I can read it now, but in order to confirm if I wrote the document or not, I really am not able to do that. My initials are not there. Each one of my documents bears my initials. In order for me to protect myself, I would put my initials on each document I drafted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just scroll down to the bottom of these two pages. And the B/C/S, please. Now, Mr. Softic, is it reasonable to assume that this document was sent nowhere? It hasn't got any markings at the end of it, markings from the Communication Centre, to say that it was received by the Communications Centre and who it was sent to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if this is an outgoing document -- well, even if it's an incoming document, it would have to have a marking that it had been received in the Communications Centre or that it was sent from the Communications Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does it have such marking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not see any here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we then assume that it was never in nor outgoing, incoming nor outgoing? Perhaps it was never even drafted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just see whether it was incoming or outgoing on the basis of the top of the document. If I were to be shown the top of the document, then I could see whether it was outgoing or incoming. Now I cannot, on the basis of -- this document did not even have to be sent through the centre. You see, some mail went by courier, messenger. Whether this was dispatched in some other way, I don't know. However, as far as I can see, this is an outgoing document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, are you then saying that there are other ways, other than the Communications Centre, through which documents could be dispatched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if there are such ways, it is therefore possible for a document to be dispatched without it having markings at the bottom like this one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If a messenger carried it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. As long as it hasn't gone through the Communications Centre, it is possible, like this one -- like you're saying this one didn't go via the Communications Centre and this one doesn't have markings. It is possible for documents to be dispatched without them having markings on them, like through the courier, as you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could have been sent, but it would have had to have been recorded at the destination, where it had been sent originally. So if this was sent to the 3rd Corps, in the 3rd Corps every document would have to be recorded, regardless of whether it arrived through the Communications Centre or by courier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, you have introduced the mode of dispatch through a courier to explain the absence of markings on this document; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, and I'm just asking you: Is it therefore possible that documents could be dispatched from your office other than through the Communications Centre; as a result of which, there would be no markings on the bottom of the document, e.g., through a courier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it also possible, therefore, that the previous document that we were talking about, which didn't have markings, could have been sent through a courier, hence the absence of markings on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's possible, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, you may proceed, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Mr. Softic, please, do you agree that the 3rd Corps had its headquarters in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And that Sarajevo was under siege?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It is not possible to send such documents by courier, especially in that kind of situation; right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: With great difficulty, hardly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: First and foremost, I wish to establish the following, and let's see whether you'll agree with me. Couriers were used mostly within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, within Sarajevo. A courier was within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Vis a vis the 3rd Corps, and to the 3rd Corps documents went through Communications; right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Through communications centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: There was not a single reason for this document not to be sent through Communications, rather to be sent by courier?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: For this particular document, I see no special reason why it would be sent by courier. It should have been sent through the Communications Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Now I'm going to ask you something that has to do with IKM Kakanj, and I'll go back to the Operations Centre of the Supreme Command. You mentioned that there was a command post at Kakanj that had been established, and now I want to ask you the following: The Supreme Command Staff could not have functioned efficiently as they operated from Sarajevo that was under siege?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I just wish to ask you the following: Could you tell the Honourable Trial Chamber, how far away is Sarajevo from Zenica, where the headquarters of the 3rd Corps was, in kilometres, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, but I think it's about 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. And there were no buses, trains, traffic was absolutely impossible because of combat operations and because of the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now could the witness please be shown document D208. For the transcript, it's a document of the Supreme Command Staff, Sarajevo, dated the 26th of November, 1993. It is entitled "Relocation of the Supreme Command Staff Order."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to just look at the introductory part of this document. It says -- just read it, please. You don't have to read it out loud. I want to put some questions to you in relation to that. Do you agree that the Supreme Command Staff had assessed that in order to ensure uninterrupted functioning of command and control over combat operations on the ground, it was necessary to relocate a large part of the Supreme Command Staff from Sarajevo to territory outside Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree that this was the area of Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Kakanj is about 40 kilometres away from Sarajevo; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Approximately, I think so. Maybe it's a bit more; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your Honour, could this document please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 279.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, could you please repeat the number, because the interpreter did not hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D242. For the transcript, this is a document of the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces, dated the 2nd of January, 1994, and it is entitled "Order for the SVK to go out to the Command Post," submitted to -- et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Please, just have a look at this. You see the first sentence underneath "Order": "The Supreme Command Staff will go out to the new command post on the 5th of January, 1994." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: What I wish to ask you, in relation to this, is the following: This order was carried out; right? I mean, I'm asking you about the Supreme Command Staff. A large part of it actually left --

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this document please be assigned an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 280.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like you to look at document D241. Again, this is a document of the Supreme Command Staff, dated the 16th of February, 1994, entitled "Organisation of the deployment of the Supreme Command Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Please look at this document. Please look at the introductory part. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Could it please be zoomed in a bit so I can see it better?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Bosnian version, please, could it be zoomed in?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Have a look at this, at the introductory part. You will agree that it speaks about the indispensability of the Supreme Command Staff being out in the field? Then please look at paragraph 1 of the order, it relocates the following: "In order to improve its functioning, the responsibility, its place, and role in waging armed combat and commanding and controlling, it is being relocated to the area of Kakanj."

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Please look at the first subparagraph or, rather, 1(b). You see there is 1(a) and then there's 1(b)?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I can hardly see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can hardly see it. Your Honour, I can give a hard copy of this document in Bosnian to the witness, because it is legible in hard copy but not on the screen. Could you please just give this to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: So we're talking about 1(b). Please take a look. I'm going to quote it: "The Operations Centre for the planning, preparation, organisation, monitoring and commanding of combat operations, according to establishment." Please take a look. This regulates the following: That parts of the Supreme Command Staff are being relocated, and this included the Operations Centre, according to establishment; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: In other words, this Operations Centre was moved to Kakanj in its entirety; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: All activities related to combat operations took place in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: The Operations Centre was duty-bound to follow combat operations and the overall situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: General Delic, with a smaller number of his staff and his Cabinet, remained in Sarajevo; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: He went into Kakanj every now and then; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: He went to Kakanj every now and then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you tell us how often this actually happened?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I think he went to Kakanj from time to time. When he went to Kakanj, he often stayed outside Kakanj in the field with the units in corps. I just know one thing, that when I'd look for him to tell him something, that I could find him in Kakanj very rarely. Usually, I would leave messages in relation to some information that I would have to deal with; that is to say, establishing contact with him was very difficult for me. It was really very difficult for me because he was on the move, he was not just in one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that he would leave Sarajevo very briefly, for two- or three-day stints only, and then he would go back?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Well, was it two or three days or more, I don't know, but it was always for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, could this document please be assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 281.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise. Let me just find the number that the Prosecutor used today, or, rather, can the witness please be shown Exhibit 274 that the Prosecutor showed him today, please, E274.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Exhibit 274, please look at the first page. The Command of the 3rd Corps from Zenica sends this document, and then there's this first part here. Could that please be enlarged, the Bosnian version, where the stamp is, where it says: "Keep until the end." Do you agree it says "SVK of the Armed Forces" and that you can slightly discern "KM Kakanj"?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, "SVK of the Armed Forces," and the rest, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you. Could this document please be shown -- or, rather, page 4 of this document, could it be shown, please? The fourth page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you agree that here there is a mark indicating receipt at the Kakanj Supreme Command Staff and that it was dispatched and received at the Kakanj SVK; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that it was received at the SVK Kakanj at 0020 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: So the document was not received in Sarajevo; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was received at the SVK Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you this now: It's correct, isn't it, that from the point in time when the Operations Centre was transferred to Kakanj, the Supreme Command and the Supreme Command Staff only received summary reports from Kakanj, not the original versions of reports from the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you. The fact that this document was received in Kakanj does not necessarily mean that General Delic ever saw it?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: This does not mean that General Delic ever saw this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, we can put this document away. I would like to ask you something else now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ten minutes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that I will be finished very soon, perhaps in five minutes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, you said that the situation in Sarajevo was very difficult; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It was difficult not only because of the siege by the Serbian forces, but also because of internal misunderstandings within the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, because of internal problems, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you agree the situation culminated in July 1993 when the Supreme Command Staff was attacked, as well as various police stations throughout town?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. Perhaps it was in the month of June, but I do recall that the situation culminated around that time, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I would like the witness to look at D239. It's an order by the Supreme Command Staff of the 25th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Witness, we can see that this is a document of the Commander's Cabinet, drafted in the Commander's Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can you please scroll the document down more, more, so that I can see the signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can we look at page 2 for the witness. Please, can you look at this "Trebevic," please, before it disappears, you can look at "Trebevic" and "Trebevic-2."

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, and it's mentioned on page 2 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: All right. Do you see down there the signature and stamp of General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Please, you knew that an order was drafted in the Cabinet or, rather, that General Delic took certain steps in order to resolve the situation of crime in Sarajevo; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't know any details. All I knew was just information. I was not informed about all the details, but I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I'm not going to go into the details with you. All I'm asking is if you knew about this order from General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that I did know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, please, please, you know -- look at item 5, please. Look where it says that: "Use all means at your disposal, including weapons, to bring in Musan Topalovic, Ramiz Delalic, and others if there is any resistance or opposition"?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: You knew that such an order was issued?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you agree that this was carried out?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, from what I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you agree that many people after this action were arrested by the military organs?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Many of them were brought to trial after that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And these criminal proceedings are being conducted to this very day in relation to these very events?

utterances.speaker: MURAT SOFTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, can this document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
